sentences.text: Senhora Aurora at the top house, who was eighty-one and had lived up there her whole life, called a meeting in her kitchen, which meant four adults, Duarte, and Duarte's little sister who was asleep on a chair by nine, which nobody remarked on because she was six and six-year-olds get theirs early wherever they live.
They went through the options.
It should be said that this was, by the standards of Casal do Meio, an extraordinary event.
There had never been a meeting about the donkey.

In two hundred years of that hill, as far as any of them could establish, nobody had ever sat down in a kitchen and discussed her out loud with other adults present, and all four of them were visibly uncomfortable about doing it.
The first was to move down.
This is not as ridiculous as it sounds — there were two empty houses in the middle that week — and it was rejected in under a minute by everybody, and Duarte noticed that nobody gave a reason.
The second was to go down and meet her.
Senhora Aurora's son-in-law had tried this on the Tuesday: had walked down at half nine and stood at the terrace, in the road, and waited for her to come past.
He said that she had come past.
He said that she had gone round him.
He said, with some difficulty, that he had walked back up feeling exactly as awake as when he set out, and that he was not going to try it again and would rather not discuss it.
Duarte asked him one question about it, weeks later, when the whole business was over, and got one answer.
He asked what it had been like when she went round him.
The son-in-law thought about it and said: "Like being furniture." The third was to do something about the foot.
That was Duarte's, and it got the reaction that ideas from twelve-year-olds get in a room of adults, which is a pause and then somebody else saying it again slightly differently eleven minutes later.
The trouble with the third option was that nobody in Casal do Meio had ever touched her.
There was no tradition of it.
She was not anybody's donkey and had never been in anybody's field and did not, as far as anyone knew, exist during the day.

Senhora Aurora said that her mother had told her that you leave her alone and she comes, and that in eighty-one years she had never heard of anybody trying anything else, and that there was probably a reason for that.
Duarte asked what the reason was.
Senhora Aurora said she had no idea and that this was exactly the sort of question that had made his grandfather difficult.
She said it warmly, and Duarte took it as a compliment, and it was probably meant as one.

The meeting broke up at about eleven with nothing decided and four adults going home to houses in which they were about to lie awake, and Duarte's mother put a hand on the back of his neck on the way out of the door and did not say anything, which in that family was a whole conversation.
